questions.q: What engine powers Dataflow Gen2 in Fabric?
options: Power Query, the same engine behind Excel and Power BI dataflows
Apache Spark, the same engine as mapping data flows
A brand-new proprietary engine unrelated to any existing Microsoft tool
T-SQL exclusively
questions.explain: Dataflow Gen2 is built on Power Query, not Spark — a genuinely different engine from the mapping data flows covered in Chapter 5.

questions.q: Why does Dataflow Gen2's Power Query foundation matter for who can use it?
options: It makes it accessible to Power Query-literate analysts, not just Spark-literate engineers
It requires exactly the same skill set as mapping data flows
It means only professional developers can use it
Power Query has no bearing on who can author dataflows
questions.explain: Because Dataflow Gen2 uses the same engine as Power BI and Excel's Power Query, report authors already familiar with it can be productive quickly — a different audience than Spark-based tools typically reach.

questions.q: How did classic Power BI dataflows (Gen1) differ from Dataflow Gen2 in terms of output destinations?
options: Gen1 only stored data in its own internal storage; Gen2 supports multiple external destinations
Gen1 and Gen2 support exactly the same destinations
Gen2 can only write to Power BI's internal storage, unlike Gen1
Neither Gen1 nor Gen2 supports any output destinations
questions.explain: Dataflow Gen2 significantly expanded destination options beyond Gen1's internal-only storage, including Fabric-native options like Lakehouse Tables and Warehouse.

questions.q: Which two destination types are Fabric-native and didn't exist as mapping data flow sink options in classic ADF?
options: Fabric Lakehouse Tables and Fabric Warehouse
Azure Blob Storage and Azure SQL Database
SharePoint Files and Snowflake
None — the destination options are identical between both tools
questions.explain: Fabric Lakehouse Tables and Fabric Warehouse are Fabric-native destinations that simply didn't exist as connector types in classic ADF's mapping data flows.

questions.q: When might mapping data flows (or Spark notebooks) still be preferable to Dataflow Gen2?
options: For heavy, large-scale join-and-aggregate transformations across huge datasets
Dataflow Gen2 is strictly better in every scenario with no tradeoffs
Mapping data flows are being deprecated with no Fabric equivalent
Only when working entirely outside of Fabric
questions.explain: Spark's real strengths still suit heavy, large-scale transformations better than Power Query's model, which fits wrangling and exploratory cleanup tasks more naturally.
